summary: Describes the encapsulation of IEEE 802.2 LLC PDUs, and by extension IP and ARP, on HIPPI, a high-speed interface. It was replaced by RFC 2834.

plainLanguage.summary: HIPPI is a very fast cable used for big computers. This document says how to put Internet packets in the right envelope for it.

questions: how does ip work on hippi
subtitle: How to send Internet Protocol packets over high-speed HIPPI connections.

tldr.problem: HIPPI is a very high-speed point-to-point or switched connection (800 Mbps or 1600 Mbps), used mainly by supercomputers and research centers. The ANSI standards defined the physical layer but left the networking aspects undefined, so there was no standard way to run IP on HIPPI.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1374 defines how to encapsulate IP and ARP packets in HIPPI protocol structures. It specifies the packet format using HIPPI-FP (frame protocol) and HIPPI-LE (link encapsulation) headers, address resolution methods, and rules for managing connections.
tldr.outcome: Organizations could now run standard IP networking over HIPPI switches, allowing high-speed LANs for supercomputers and special-purpose networks. RFC 2834 later replaced this with an updated version.

today: RFC 1374 was published as a Proposed Standard in October 1992. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2834, which reflects experience with HIPPI deployments and provides clarifications and improvements.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The ANSI High-Performance Parallel Interface (HIPPI) is a simplex (one-way) data channel capable of transmitting nearly 800 megabits per second, or 1600 megabits per second with the 64-bit option. Configured in pairs, HIPPI provides simultaneous send and receive capability. Between 1987 and 1991, the ANSI X3T9.3 HIPPI working group produced standards for the physical specification (HIPPI-PH), the frame format (HIPPI-FP), the encapsulation of IEEE 802.2 LLC (HIPPI-LE), and switch behavior (HIPPI-SC).

HIPPI switches can connect computers and peripherals for many purposes, but the ANSI working group stopped short of describing their use as Local Area Networks. RFC 1374 extends the ANSI standards to describe how HIPPI-SC switches function as LANs, how to run the Internet Protocol on HIPPI, and how address resolution works. The guiding principle is that IP datagrams on HIPPI should be identical to those on conventional networks, except for the HIPPI-specific framing overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: HIPPI is a cable for very fast computers. Nobody had explained how to send Internet packets over HIPPI, so this document fills that gap.

sections.title: HIPPI Architecture and Equipment
sections.content:
A HIPPI network consists of nodes (computers with HIPPI interfaces), cables or serial links, HIPPI-SC switches, and possibly gateways to other networks. Each node has one pair of HIPPI links, one for sending and one for receiving.

HIPPI switches are non-blocking, meaning there is always a path available from any source to any destination on a single switch. When the network contains multiple switches, a link between switches may be shared by multiple source/destination pairs, creating a blocking network. RFC 1374 assumes single-switch or simple multi-switch networks where blocking is not a problem.

Each HIPPI port can operate at either 32-bit (800 Mbps) or 64-bit (1600 Mbps) width. Nodes must be able to select the appropriate width at the start of each new connection. The payload is organized in bursts, and a connection can consist of multiple packets, up to a limit of 68 bursts per connection to ensure fair sharing when multiple nodes contend for the same destination.
sections.plainLanguage: A HIPPI network is like a telephone switchboard where very fast computers plug in. Each computer has a pair of cables: one to send, one to receive. The switch makes sure everyone gets a fair turn.

sections.title: Packet Format and Encapsulation
sections.content:
An IP datagram sent over HIPPI is wrapped in multiple headers. From the bottom up: the HIPPI-FP (Frame Protocol) header is 8 octets, the HIPPI-LE (Link Encapsulation) header is 24 octets, the IEEE 802.2 LLC/SNAP header is 8 octets, and finally the IP or ARP datagram follows.

The HIPPI-FP header identifies the content as LLC data (ULP-id = 4) and specifies the size of the encapsulation header and the IP data. The HIPPI-LE header contains the message type, source and destination switch addresses, and source and destination IEEE 48-bit MAC addresses. The IEEE 802.2 LLC header uses the standard values (SSAP and DSAP both 170 decimal) and Unnumbered Information (CTL = 3). The SNAP portion sets the EtherType field to indicate IP (2048) or ARP (2054).

After the IP or ARP data, fill octets are added as needed to make the total packet a multiple of 8 octets, as required by HIPPI-LE. The maximum transmission unit (MTU) for HIPPI-SC LANs is defined as 65,280 octets, allowing an IP packet to fit in a 64K buffer with room for future expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet is like a letter in multiple envelopes. The outer envelope says 'I am sending data.' The next envelope says 'Here is where the data goes.' The next says 'This is Internet data.' Finally, the letter itself is the IP packet.

sections.title: Address Resolution on HIPPI
sections.content:
HIPPI networks use two types of hardware addresses: IEEE 48-bit Universal LAN MAC addresses (ULAs) and 12-bit or 24-bit HIPPI-SC Switch Addresses. The RFC uses standard ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) but extends it to also resolve Switch Addresses.

When a node wants to communicate with another node, it must learn three mappings: IP address to ULA, ULA to Switch Address, and the 12-bit Switch Address to use in the I-field. The RFC defines address resolution message types: AR_Request and AR_Response for standard ARP, and AR_S_Request and AR_S_Response for self-address resolution (a node discovering its own Switch Address).

Address resolution can be implemented in three ways: (1) as a distributed function if the switch supports multicast, with nodes responding to their own ARP requests; (2) using a third-party ARP agent that replies on behalf of other nodes; or (3) using static address mappings configured by the network administrator. Piggybacking ARP requests on HIPPI-LE address resolution packets allows the two protocols to work together as a single operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Nodes need to learn each other's addresses: IP addresses, hardware addresses, and switch port numbers. ARP handles this, but HIPPI adds an extra layer to also discover the switch port.

sections.title: Connection Management and Fairness
sections.content:
HIPPI requires careful rules to ensure fair access when multiple nodes contend for the same destination. A source may hold a connection for up to 68 bursts, regardless of how many packets are sent; if the burst count reaches the limit, the connection must be released. This prevents one node from monopolizing a popular destination.

Sources should minimize connection switching time, as the time between the end of one connection and the start of the next reduces network throughput. A 10-microsecond gap allows nearly full HIPPI throughput with large packets; a 60-microsecond gap reduces throughput by about 10 percent.

A Camp-on feature in the I-field allows a source to wait for a destination to become available rather than repeatedly retrying the connection. Without Camp-on, the source cannot tell whether a rejection came from the destination or the switch, and cannot distinguish between temporary busy conditions and actual errors. With Camp-on, most rejections indicate an error condition that warrants logging.
sections.plainLanguage: Many computers might want to talk to the same big computer at once. HIPPI makes sure nobody talks too long, so everyone gets a fair turn.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: RFC 1374 was published as a Proposed Standard in October 1992. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2834, which provides an updated version accounting for experience with HIPPI deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is old and has been replaced by a newer version (RFC 2834) that fixes issues found in real-world use.
